name: Focusing light underwater
scope: The problem: underwater, the cornea can't bend light (water and eye-fluid have nearly the same refractive index), so aquatic eyes must do all their focusing with the lens. T1: a fish's eye lens is a hard, near-perfect SPHERE (not the squishy disc land animals have). T2: fish focus by MOVING the whole rigid lens back and forth (retractor lentis muscle), like sliding a slide-projector lens, instead of squeezing it to change shape as we do. T3: the octopus — a mollusk on a totally separate evolutionary branch — built the SAME camera-style eye with a spherical lens it also moves to focus (a textbook case of convergent evolution). T4: the fish lens fixes spherical aberration with a graded refractive index — denser in the center than the edge (Matthiessen's ratio, focal length ~2.5x lens radius) — so a clear image forms across the whole sphere.
source: Land & Nilsson, 'Animal Eyes' (2012); Kroger on Matthiessen's ratio; standard vertebrate-eye physiology
framing_note: Every rung's answer is a concrete eye-mechanics fact about a specific animal (fish sphere-lens, fish sliding focus, octopus convergent eye, graded-index sphere). The spine is 'how do you focus light where a cornea is useless.' Lead with the scene (a fish's or octopus's eye), never 'What is a lens?' The octopus rung is the dinner-test payoff: two unrelated animals independently invented the same eye. Accuracy: the octopus eye is convergent, NOT inherited from a shared eyed-ancestor; say 'built the same solution' not 'related.'

name: Eyeshine and seeing in the dark
scope: The night-vision toolkit, one animal per rung. T1: the greenish-gold glow of a cat's or deer's eyes in headlights is a mirror behind the retina — the tapetum lucidum — bouncing light back through the retina for a second chance to catch it. T2: cats' retinas are packed with rods (dim-light cells) and almost no cones, trading color for sensitivity. T3: the tarsier, a tiny primate, has each eyeball BIGGER than its brain to gather every scrap of moonlight (and, oddly, tarsiers LOST the tapetum, so the giant eye is their whole answer). T4: deep-sea fish evolve enormous tubular eyes; some deep-sea sharks and the reindeer even shift their tapetum's COLOR seasonally (reindeer eyes turn from gold in summer to blue in winter, scattering more dim light). T5: the colossal squid holds the record for the largest eye of any animal — a dinner-plate ~27 cm — tuned to spot the faint glow that sperm whales stir up in the black deep.
source: Warrant & Nilsson on nocturnal vision; Stokkan et al. 2013 (reindeer tapetum colour shift, Proc. R. Soc. B); Nilsson et al. on colossal squid eye size
framing_note: Scene-led: the glowing eyes in headlights, the tarsier's saucer eyes. Each answer is a named structure or a named animal's extreme (tapetum, rod-packed retina, tarsier eye-bigger-than-brain, reindeer color-shift, colossal squid record eye). Reindeer blue-winter-eye is the standout dinner fact — attribute to the 2013 study. Note the tarsier LACKS a tapetum so its giant eye is the compensation — don't stack both traits on one animal as if they co-occur.

name: Compound eyes and the insect mosaic
scope: How thousands of tiny eyes make one picture. T1: a dragonfly's or fly's eye is really a bundle of thousands of separate tubes (ommatidia) — up to ~30,000 in a dragonfly — each seeing one dot, so the image is a mosaic, not a smooth photo. T2: compound eyes are terrible at fine detail but brilliant at DETECTING MOTION, which is why a fly dodges the swat — its flicker-fusion rate is so fast our slow hand looks like slow motion to it. T3: a dragonfly's near-wraparound eyes give it almost 360-degree vision, and it aims interceptions using motion-tracking neurons that predict where prey will be. T4: the mantis shrimp's compound eye is the strangest — each eye scans on its own stalk and has a special 6-row band; it carries up to 16 photoreceptor classes (12 for color, several for UV, plus polarized-light detectors).
source: Land & Nilsson 'Animal Eyes'; Thoen et al. 2014 Science (mantis shrimp photoreceptors); dragonfly interception-neuron work (Gonzalez-Bellido/Wiederman)
framing_note: Anchor the mantis-shrimp rung ONLY on eye anatomy (16 receptor classes, scanning stalks) — its color-vision surprise gets its own ladder below, so don't preempt the payoff here. Fly-dodges-swat is the dinner hook: frame it as the fly perceiving time faster (flicker fusion), a real, concrete handle. Answers are named structures (ommatidia) and named animals' extremes.

name: The mantis shrimp color myth
scope: The internet legend meets the experiment. T2: the mantis shrimp famously has up to 16 photoreceptor types — 12 for color where humans have just 3 — and the myth says it must see an unimaginable rainbow. T3: the twist — a 2014 behavioral study (Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall) trained mantis shrimp to pick colors and found they're actually WORSE than humans at telling similar colors apart; they can't discriminate hues we easily separate. T4: the resolution — the shrimp doesn't compare its 12 channels the way our brain does; it appears to RECOGNIZE a color in one fast scanning sweep (a rough spectral 'barcode') rather than finely discriminate it, trading precision for speed with almost no brain-processing.
source: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall 2014, Science 343:411 ('A Different Form of Color Vision in Mantis Shrimp')
framing_note: This is a myth-busting ladder — the payoff IS that the famous 'best color vision on Earth' claim is wrong. Accuracy is the whole point: the mechanism is RECOGNITION, not discrimination; state it as the 2014 study's finding and flag it as an active-research reinterpretation, not a settled cold fact. Answer to the pivotal rung is the vivid action ('scans and recognizes in one sweep'), not a number. Do NOT let a choice imply mantis shrimp 'see more colors' — that's the busted myth.

name: Seeing colors we can't (ultraviolet)
scope: The invisible-to-us channel, animal by animal. T2: bees see ULTRAVIOLET, and many flowers wear UV 'nectar guides' — bullseye patterns invisible to us that scream 'land here' to a bee. T3: many BIRDS are tetrachromats with a fourth (UV/violet) cone, so plumage that looks plain to us can blaze with UV signals — e.g. male and female blue tits look identical to us but the male's crown glows in UV. T4: reindeer see into the UV, which helps in the arctic winter — lichen (food) and wolf fur (danger) ABSORB UV and show up as dark shapes against UV-bright snow. T4b: the swordtail/guppy and mantis-shrimp world uses UV signals too, and some butterflies have UV wing patches that flag mates — a whole social channel hidden from human eyes.
source: Chittka on bee UV/flower guides; Hunt et al. on avian UV cones; Hogg et al. 2011 (reindeer UV vision, Proc. R. Soc. B)
framing_note: Each rung reveals ONE animal's hidden channel with a concrete payoff (bee sees the flower's landing-strip; blue tit's secret UV crown; reindeer sees wolf-fur as a dark shape on snow). Reindeer-UV-wolf is the dinner winner. Keep answers to named animals and the vivid thing they see; avoid abstract 'they see UV' with no scene. Accuracy: 'UV nectar guides' are real photographed patterns — fine to state as fact.

name: Predator eyes vs prey eyes
scope: Where an animal's eyes sit tells you whether it hunts or is hunted. T1: eyes on the FRONT (owl, cat, wolf, human) give overlapping fields and depth perception for judging the pounce — 'eyes in front, the animal hunts.' T2: eyes on the SIDES (rabbit, horse, deer) sacrifice depth for a near-360-degree watch, so a grazer spots the ambush from any angle — 'eyes on the side, the animal hides.' T3: the goat/sheep horizontal rectangular pupil rotates to stay level with the ground even when the head lowers to graze, keeping the whole horizon in focus for predators. T4: some predators break the rule — the woodcock (prey) has eyes so far back it sees a full 360 including behind its own head, while the chameleon aims two independently-swiveling turret eyes, scanning separately then locking BOTH forward for a stereo strike at its tongue's target.
source: Banks et al. 2015 (pupil shape & ecology, Science Advances); standard comparative visual-ecology; chameleon binocular-strike literature
framing_note: The 'front=hunt / side=hide' rhyme is the recognition base — great T1/T2 anchor for the ~30% low-tier target. Answers are the placement-and-payoff (depth for pouncing; wide watch for spotting ambush; level horizontal pupil; chameleon's swivel-then-lock). Chameleon rung stays on the EYE trick (independent turrets → binocular strike), not the tongue mechanics (that's a feeding ladder). Concrete over jargon: 'overlapping fields' > 'binocular stereopsis.'

name: The strangest eyes in the animal kingdom
scope: Eyes that break the rules of how an eye should work. T2: the scallop has up to ~200 tiny blue eyes along its mantle edge, and each one focuses with a curved MIRROR of guanine crystals behind the retina — not a lens — the same trick used in some telescopes. T3: the four-eyed fish (Anableps) swims at the surface with each eye split by a band into an upper half for seeing in AIR and a lower half for seeing in WATER at the same time. T3b: the barreleye fish has a transparent, fluid-filled dome for a forehead and two tubular green eyes that rotate UP inside its own see-through skull to watch for prey silhouettes overhead. T4: the brownsnout spookfish is the only vertebrate known to focus with a MIRROR as well as a lens; and the ogre-faced (net-casting) spider has two huge lenses so light-hungry it rebuilds the light-sensitive membrane fresh each night.
source: Palmer et al. 2017 (scallop mirror eyes, Science); Anableps optics; MBARI barreleye (Robison & Reisenbichler 2008); Wagner et al. (spookfish mirror eye, Current Biology 2009)
framing_note: Pure wonder ladder — every answer is a named animal doing something visibly impossible (scallop's 200 mirror eyes, fish that sees air and water at once, fish with a see-through head and eyes that rotate inside it). These are the dinner-test all-stars; keep the stem building the scene so the strange fact IS the answer. Accuracy: scallop and spookfish mirror-optics are real published findings — safe as fact; barreleye rotating eyes are confirmed by MBARI footage.

name: Echolocation, built twice
scope: Seeing with sound, in two unrelated groups. T1: a bat hunting in total darkness screams high-pitched clicks (mostly above human hearing) and reads the echoes to map moths in mid-air — hearing shapes, not seeing them. T2: dolphins and toothed whales echolocate too, sending clicks from a fatty forehead organ (the MELON) and picking up echoes through their lower jawbone. T3: convergence proof — bats and toothed whales evolved echolocation entirely separately, yet a hearing gene (Prestin/the protein in outer-hair-cells) changed in the SAME way in both, a striking case of the same molecular answer arriving twice. T4: the sperm whale drives the loudest biological sound on Earth — clicks up to ~230 dB from the huge spermaceti organ in its head — used to scan for squid a kilometre down in the black. T5: bats fine-tune with Doppler — the horseshoe bat shifts its call frequency to cancel its own speed, so a fluttering moth's wingbeat stands out as a tiny frequency flicker in the returning echo.
source: Griffin (bat echolocation); Au 'The Sonar of Dolphins'; Liu et al. 2010 & Parker et al. 2013 (Prestin convergence, Nature); Madsen et al. on sperm-whale click levels; Schnitzler on horseshoe-bat Doppler
framing_note: Spine = 'map the world with sound.' Every rung a named animal's concrete mechanism (bat clicks, dolphin melon + jaw hearing, Prestin gene twice, sperm-whale loudest click, horseshoe-bat Doppler). The Prestin convergence rung is the intellectual payoff — same gene changed the same way in bat and whale; state it as the finding of the 2010/2013 papers. Numbers (230 dB) allowed only because the stem constructs 'loudest animal sound.' Keep dolphin melon and jaw-hearing as the two-part concrete handle, not jargon.

name: Infrasound and hearing through the feet
scope: The deep sounds below human hearing, and feeling the ground. T2: elephants rumble to each other in INFRASOUND — pitches too low for us to hear — that roll across the savanna for miles. T3: elephants also 'hear' these calls through the GROUND: seismic vibrations travel through their feet and up the leg bones to the inner ear (they detectably freeze, lean, and orient toward distant seismic rumbles). T3b: the giraffe and other big animals hum at night in low frequencies; whales like the fin and blue whale sing the lowest, farthest-traveling calls of any animal, crossing whole ocean basins. T4: many animals feel ground vibration to survive — elephant-shrews, kangaroo rats, and golden moles drum or read substrate vibrations; the case is clearest in the elephant, whose seismic sense may warn it of distant storms or stampedes before any airborne sound arrives.
source: O'Connell-Rodwell on elephant seismic communication (Proc. R. Soc. B); Payne on elephant infrasound; blue/fin whale low-frequency song literature
framing_note: Answers stay concrete: the elephant rumbling below human hearing, the elephant reading ground-shakes through its feet-and-bones, the whale song crossing an ocean. Seismic-through-feet is the dinner payoff — attribute the sensing pathway (feet to leg bones to ear) as the studied hypothesis, not folklore. Avoid the over-claimed 'elephants predicted the tsunami' anecdote as fact; keep it to demonstrated seismic detection.

name: The lateral line  -  feeling the water move
scope: The 'sixth sense' running down a fish's flank. T2: the faint line you can see stretching head-to-tail on a fish is a row of sense organs (the lateral line) that feels water MOVING against the body — a sense of distant touch. T3: tiny hair-cell bundles inside it (neuromasts) bend when water flows past, letting a fish feel an approaching predator, a wall, or the wake of a neighbor without seeing it. T3b: this is how a whole SCHOOL turns as one in the dark — each fish feels its neighbors' pressure waves and matches them, no leader needed. T4: the blind Mexican cave fish, living in lightless caves, has an extra-sensitive lateral line and 'reads' the water bouncing off cave walls to swim without bumping — echolocation-by-touch. T4b: the same hair-cell system, moved inside the head, became the inner ear of every vertebrate — your sense of hearing and balance descends from a fish's lateral line.
source: Coombs & Montgomery 'The Hydrodynamics of the Lateral Line'; Bleckmann on schooling; Yoshizawa on Astyanax cave-fish lateral line
framing_note: Each answer is a concrete fish ability the lateral line grants (feel the predator's wake, school in the dark, the cave fish reading walls). The evolutionary payoff rung (lateral line → your inner ear) is a genuine dinner-test 'whoa' — state it as the accepted homology. Keep 'neuromast' introduced in plain terms (water-sensing hair bundle); don't assume the jargon (teach-before-test).

name: Ears at the extremes
scope: Hearing pushed to the edge. T2: the barn owl hunts in pitch dark by SOUND alone; its two ear openings sit at different HEIGHTS (one higher than the other), so a mouse's rustle reaches them at slightly different times AND loudness, pinpointing the prey in both left-right and up-down. T3: the owl's flat, dish-shaped face is a sound-funnel (a feather 'facial ruff') that channels the faintest noise to those offset ears, and it can strike a mouse in total darkness from the sound alone. T3b: the great gray owl plunges through a foot of snow onto voles it never sees, locating them purely by the sound under the surface. T4: an evolutionary arms race in the air — many moths evolved simple EARS just to hear bat sonar and dive away; some tiger moths jam the bat's clicks with ultrasonic clicks of their own, and one moth wears sound-absorbing fuzz that makes it nearly invisible to sonar (acoustic stealth). T5: the greater wax moth is claimed to hear the highest frequencies known in nature (up to ~300 kHz), likely an over-evolved defense to stay ahead of bat calls.
source: Konishi on barn-owl sound localization; Corcoran & Conner 2009 Science (tiger-moth sonar jamming); Neil et al. 2020 (moth acoustic-stealth fur, PNAS); Moir et al. on wax-moth hearing range
framing_note: Answers are named-animal hearing feats (owl's offset ears, dish-face funnel, great gray owl through snow, moths that jam or absorb sonar). The moth-vs-bat arms race is the payoff — each move is concrete (evolve an ear, jam with clicks, wear stealth fuzz). Attribute the wax-moth ~300 kHz record as the reported study finding, not a settled superlative. Numbers only where the stem builds the 'highest ever' frame.

name: Super-smellers
scope: Noses that read the world in chemistry. T1: a dog's nose carries on the order of 300 million scent receptors to a human's ~6 million, and a bigger slice of its brain is devoted to smell — it doesn't just smell more, it smells in far finer detail. T2: a dog smells in STEREO — each nostril samples independently and it can tell which side a scent came from — and it exhales out the SIDE slits so the outgoing breath doesn't blow away the scent it's sniffing. T3: sharks track prey by smell across huge distances and can detect blood/amino acids at tiny concentrations; they steer toward a smell by comparing the TIMING of when odor hits each nostril (nostril the smell reaches first = turn that way), not merely which side is stronger. T4: the bear beats them all on land — a grizzly's sense of smell is estimated many times a bloodhound's and can find a carcass from miles away; the elephant may have the most odor-receptor GENES of any animal (~2,000, roughly double a dog's), letting it sort scents in astonishing detail with its trunk.
source: Craven et al. on canine olfaction; Gardiner & Atema 2010 (shark odor timing steering, Current Biology); Niimura et al. 2014 (elephant olfactory-receptor genes, Genome Research)
framing_note: Each answer is a concrete smelling superpower of one animal (dog stereo-nose + side-vented breath, shark steering by odor timing, elephant's record receptor genes). The shark 'turn toward whichever nostril the smell hits first' is the surprising, studied mechanism (Gardiner & Atema) — use it, don't default to the myth of 'a drop of blood in an Olympic pool.' Numbers (300M receptors, ~2000 genes) are allowed because the stem constructs the comparison. Bear/elephant estimates: frame as 'estimated,' not exact.

name: Tasting with the whole body
scope: Taste organs in the strangest places. T2: the catfish is basically a swimming TONGUE — its whole skin, and especially its barbel 'whiskers,' is covered in taste buds (a big catfish can carry over 100,000, more than any other animal), so it tastes a food pellet the instant it brushes any part of its body in muddy, dark water. T3: butterflies and flies TASTE WITH THEIR FEET — chemoreceptors on the tarsi let a butterfly stand on a leaf and instantly know if it's the right plant to lay eggs on, and a fly extends its tongue the moment its feet touch sugar. T3b: the octopus tastes by TOUCH — each sucker is lined with chemoreceptors, so an octopus 'tastes' whatever its arm touches inside a crevice without seeing it; recent work found special receptor proteins in the suckers tuned to detect prey chemicals. T4: snakes 'taste' the air with the forked tongue — flicking it collects scent particles and delivers them to the two-pronged vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ in the roof of the mouth; the FORK gives a left-right reading so the snake can follow a scent trail like a stereo nose.
source: Caprio on catfish taste-bud counts; Dethier on insect tarsal chemoreception; van Giesen et al. 2020 & Kang et al. (octopus sucker chemotactile receptors, Cell/Nature); Schwenk on snake forked-tongue trailing (Science 1994)
framing_note: Every answer is one animal's surprising taste-organ location (catfish body, butterfly feet, octopus suckers, snake forked tongue). Catfish 'swimming tongue' and butterfly 'tastes with its feet' are the dinner all-stars. Octopus sucker-taste is recent research — attribute to the 2020 receptor-protein studies. Snake fork = stereo scent-trailing (Schwenk 1994), a real finding, not just decoration. Keep numbers (100,000 taste buds) tied to the stem's 'more than any animal' frame.

name: Scent trails and the moth that smells a mate miles away
scope: Chemical messages between animals. T2: ants build highways of scent — a scout that finds food lays a PHEROMONE trail home, and the stronger the returning traffic, the stronger the trail, so the colony collectively converges on the best route (a real self-organizing algorithm engineers copied as 'ant colony optimization'). T3: a male silk/luna/emperor moth finds a female from a huge distance by smell alone — his enormous feathery antennae catch her pheromone (bombykol in the silk moth), and a male can respond to just a handful of molecules of it drifting on the wind. T3b: ants recognize nestmate-versus-intruder by a chemical 'ID badge' of cuticular hydrocarbons — a wrong smell and a foreigner is attacked; some parasites survive inside ant nests by chemically COUNTERFEITING the colony's smell. T4: alarm and defense chemistry — a crushed ant releases an alarm pheromone that rallies the nest to attack; aphids drop off a leaf when alarm-scent warns of a ladybug; and the sea's version, released 'injury' cues, sends a whole fish school scattering.
source: Holldobler & Wilson 'The Ants' / 'The Superorganism'; Butenandt et al. 1959 (bombykol, first pheromone identified); Dorigo on ant-colony optimization
framing_note: Answers are concrete chemical-signal feats (ant scent highway that self-optimizes, moth catching a few molecules on feathery antennae, ants' chemical ID badge, alarm scent scattering a colony). The moth-antenna 'a few molecules' rung is the dinner payoff — bombykol (Butenandt 1959) was the first pheromone ever identified, a nice factual anchor. Ant-highway → the copied algorithm is a genuine 'whoa.' Keep the animal the anchor; the human-tech nod (ant colony optimization) is the coherent payoff of the ant's own behavior, not an orphan.

name: Electroreception  -  reading the body electric
scope: Sensing the tiny electric fields living muscles leak. T2: sharks and rays carry jelly-filled pores around the snout — the ampullae of Lorenzini — that detect the faint electric field every heartbeat and muscle twitch of hidden prey; a shark can find a fish buried in sand by its electricity alone, and in the final strike it often closes its eyes and hunts purely by this sense. T3: the platypus hunts with its eyes, ears, AND nose sealed shut underwater, steering entirely by ~40,000 electroreceptors in its rubbery bill that pick up prey muscle-signals — pairing them with pressure sensors, it triangulates a shrimp in the dark. T4: 'weakly electric' fish like the elephantnose and the knifefish generate their OWN weak field and feel how objects DISTORT it — electric-field radar — to navigate and even 'talk' in electric pulses; the elephantnose devotes a huge share of its brain to reading these signals. T4b: the bumblebee was found to sense the weak electric CHARGE flowers carry (and even learn from it which flowers are worth visiting) — electroreception in an insect, via charge-deflected body hairs.
source: Kalmijn on elasmobranch ampullae of Lorenzini; Pettigrew on platypus bill electroreception (~40,000 receptors); Clarke et al. 2013 Science (bumblebee floral electric fields); mormyrid electrolocation literature
framing_note: Every answer is a named animal reading electricity (shark's ampullae finding buried prey, platypus hunting blind by its bill, elephantnose's self-made field-radar, bee sensing a flower's charge). Platypus-hunts-with-everything-shut is the dinner star — the ~40,000-receptor figure is stem-constructed, allowed. Bumblebee electroreception is genuine but newer — attribute to Clarke et al. 2013. Keep the platypus VENOM spur out of this ladder (different theme). Shark closing eyes on the strike is real behavior, safe to state.

name: Animals that generate electricity
scope: Living batteries. T2: the electric eel (not a true eel — it's a knifefish) stacks thousands of disc-shaped cells (electrocytes) like batteries in series down its long body; a big one can discharge a shock that has been measured near record levels. T3: a 2019 study split the electric eel into three species and found one of them, Volta's electric eel (Electrophorus voltai), can deliver ~860 volts — the strongest bioelectric shock ever recorded from any animal. T3b: the eel doesn't just stun — it can curl to bring head and tail together, concentrating the field to double the jolt, and it fires rapid volleys that make hidden prey's muscles twitch, revealing them, before a knockout blast. T4: the electric ray (torpedo ray) makes electricity in kidney-shaped organs in its 'wings' and clamps prey in an electric embrace; and one 2016 study showed an eel will leap from the water to press its shock directly into a large threat — a defense Humboldt described in 1800 (eels shocking horses) and long doubted, now confirmed on video.
source: de Santana et al. 2019 (three Electrophorus species; 860 V, Nature Communications); Catania 2014-2016 (eel doublet/curl attack & leaping defense, Science/PNAS); torpedo-ray electric-organ physiology
framing_note: Answers are the eel's/ray's concrete electrical feats (stacked electrocyte 'battery,' 860 V record, curl-to-double-the-shock, leaping shock-attack). The 860 V and three-species split are the 2019 finding — attribute the date. The 860 V is one measurement from one fish; frame as 'the strongest ever recorded,' not a routine output. The leaping-shock rung revives Humboldt's 1800 horse story, confirmed by Catania — a legitimate dinner-test human-drama payoff of the animal's real behavior. 'Not a true eel' is a fun teach-before-test correction.

name: Navigating by Earth's magnetic field
scope: The invisible compass migrating animals steer by. T2: migrating songbirds like the European robin carry an internal MAGNETIC COMPASS and can head the right way on a cloudy night with no stars or sun. T3: loggerhead sea turtle hatchlings read the ANGLE and STRENGTH of Earth's field like a coordinate grid — each stretch of coast has its own magnetic 'signature,' and a female returns decades later to nest on the very beach she hatched on, navigating by that magnetic address (natal homing). T4: the leading idea for the bird compass is astonishing — light hitting a protein (cryptochrome, likely Cry4) in the eye creates a pair of quantum-entangled radicals whose spins are nudged by the magnetic field, so the bird may literally SEE the field as a pattern across its vision. T4b: monarch butterflies use a light-dependent magnetic compass to hold their bearing on the long flight to Mexico; and animals from mole-rats to some bacteria (magnetotactic bacteria that grow tiny internal magnets) sense magnetism too.
source: Wiltschko & Wiltschko (robin magnetic compass); Lohmann on sea-turtle magnetic imprinting & natal homing; Xu et al. 2021 Nature (Cry4 magnetic sensitivity, radical-pair hypothesis); Reppert on monarch magnetoreception
framing_note: Answers are named animals reading the field (robin steering on a starless night, turtle returning to its birth beach by magnetic address, bird possibly SEEING the field via quantum radicals). Turtle natal-homing is the dinner payoff. CRITICAL accuracy: the radical-pair/cryptochrome mechanism is the leading HYPOTHESIS, not proven — frame the T4 rung as 'the leading idea' / 'scientists think,' attribute to the 2021 Cry4 work, and never state 'birds see magnetism' as settled fact. This is a flagged research-in-progress topic.

name: Seeing heat  -  the pit viper's infrared eye
scope: Sensing warmth as an image. T2: a rattlesnake, copperhead, or python has a PIT between eye and nostril that detects INFRARED — body heat — so it can strike a warm mouse in total darkness, effectively 'seeing' the animal's heat-glow. T3: how it works — the pit is a tiny air-filled chamber with an ultra-thin membrane stretched inside; the prey's warmth heats one spot on the membrane, and heat-sensing nerves fire, giving a crude thermal picture. Rattlesnake pits detect changes as small as thousandths of a degree. T3b: with a pit on EACH side of the head, the two heat-images overlap for a rough thermal depth-map, letting the snake aim a strike it can't see with its eyes. T4: the molecular trigger is TRPA1 — the same channel family that makes us feel painful heat; in pit vipers it's tuned to be the most heat-sensitive vertebrate ion channel known, converting warmth straight into a nerve signal (Gracheva et al. 2010). T4b: pythons and boas evolved heat pits SEPARATELY from vipers (their pits are rows of shallow pits along the lip, and the anatomy differs) — a convergent infrared sense arrived twice in snakes.
source: Gracheva et al. 2010 Nature (TRPA1 as the pit-organ infrared transducer); Newman & Hartline on infrared pit imaging; comparative pit anatomy (crotaline vs boid/pythonid)
framing_note: Answers are concrete pit-viper heat feats (strike a mouse in the dark by its heat, thin-membrane thermometer, two pits → thermal depth, TRPA1 the same channel as our heat-pain). The 'senses thousandths of a degree' number is stem-constructed. Convergence rung (vipers vs pythons/boas invented it separately) is a real payoff. Accuracy: the snake doesn't have a lens-image 'eye' — say it builds a crude heat-picture from a warmed membrane, not sharp vision. Attribute TRPA1 to Gracheva 2010.

name: Feeling in the dark  -  the touch specialists
scope: Animals that navigate by touch where eyes fail. T2: the star-nosed mole wears a pink 'star' of 22 fleshy tentacle-rays around its nostrils, packed with ~25,000 tiny touch organs (Eimer's organs) — it's not for smelling, it's the most sensitive touch organ known in any mammal. T3: that star makes it the FASTEST-eating mammal on Earth — it can find, identify, and swallow a worm in about a quarter of a second (~120 milliseconds), touching 10-15 spots of ground every second as it hunts blind underground. T3b: whiskers (vibrissae) are precision feelers — a seal can track the invisible wake a fish left in the water SECONDS after it passed, following the hydrodynamic trail by whisker alone; a rat sweeps its whiskers dozens of times a second to 'see' a gap's width in the dark. T4: the naked mole-rat and other burrowers rely on body hairs as trip-wire feelers along the flanks to move backward through tunnels as fast as forward; and the manatee's whiskered, prehensile snout is covered in thousands of sensory bristles to feel out plants in murky water.
